talks.title: Keynote
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Keynote.
talks.summary:
Overview: A US Cyber Command executive director delivers the CyberWarCon keynote on China's cyber threat to national security and Cyber Command's elevation from tactical to strategic operations.

Key Topics: PRC cyber threats to national security; Cyber Command's global cyberspace operations coordination; adversary economies of scale targeting backbone infrastructure; and named intrusion sets including Flax Typhoon and Volt Typhoon.

Technical Details: The speaker describes adversary focus on valid credential abuse and privileged account targeting at scale, identifying numerous PRC-associated intrusion sets targeting critical infrastructure and defense industrial base.

Takeaways: Nation-state adversaries achieve economies of scale in cyberspace targeting shared infrastructure. Defenders must prioritize credential security and backbone infrastructure protection against PRC operations.

talks.title: The Nearest Neighbor Attack: How A Russian APT Weaponized Nearby Wi-Fi Networks for Covert Access
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in The Nearest Neighbor Attack: How A Russian APT Weaponized Nearby Wi-Fi Networks for Covert Access.
talks.summary:
Talk Premise

Volexity president Stephen Adair introduces the "nearest neighbor attack," describing Russian APT use of nearby Wi-Fi for covert access based on a challenging 2022 engagement the firm can now discuss publicly.

Initial Detection

Investigation began with a custom Carbon Black Defend query flagging ser task.bat in ProgramData launching reg.exe to dump SYSTEM, SECURITY, and SAM hives into out.zip—typical credential-theft behavior on a server.

Early Timeline Clues

EDR showed an unprivileged organizational user RDP'd to the box, extracted defragment serve.zip with WinRAR GUI, and executed bundled scripts. A suspicious unsigned WaysGoose52.dll appeared under a fake Adobe directory with Print Spooler as parent process.

Forensics Response

Volexity prioritizes live memory acquisition over full disk imaging, pushing their Surge collector over RPC while continuing analysis. Adair frames the story as combining zero-day exploitation, skilled tradecraft, and innovative proximity-based access, with geopolitical espionage motivations.

talks.title: Adversarial Targeting of Critical Infrastructure Linchpins
talks.teaser: Intent explores Adversarial Targeting of Critical Infrastructure Linchpins.
talks.summary:
Three adversary tiers

Kyle Cas and colleagues profile OT/ICS threat actors at rising sophistication: Army of Russia Reborn (CAR), Cyber Avengers, and Volt Typhoon (Vanguard Panda). They use a sports analogy from freshman to varsity skill levels.

Disruption-focused groups

CAR, linked to Russian activists and poor OPSEC, brute-forces exposed VNC/HMI systems, publishes playbooks, and has caused real facility flooding and pressure manipulation. Cyber Avengers—a small IRGC-affiliated team—targets Israeli OT vendors like Unitronics, compromising perimeter devices and developing Linux ICS-oriented malware.

Strategic espionage

Volt Typhoon differs by sustained collection of OT project data, work logs, alerts, safety systems, and remediation procedures—intelligence to craft disruptive capabilities, not mere espionage. They live off the land with NPS tunnels, Impacket, web shells, and Soho router botnets, targeting interdependent fuel, water, and power providers serving military customers—the linchpins of critical infrastructure.

talks.title: RT's Covert Information Operations
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning RT's Covert Information Operations.
talks.summary:
## RT's Strategic Problem

Google Threat Analysis Group researcher Zach Butler explains how Russian state media outlet RT reaches global audiences in multiple languages but has been banned or restricted in many countries since 2014, most sharply after 2022. Losing platforms means losing reach.

## Covert Re-entry Tactics

RT responds by operating through brands that hide their affiliation. When a channel is discovered and removed, they spin up new ones. Butler documents three content strategies: original documentaries, reposted RT material with watermarks removed, and co-opted ideologically aligned influencers.

## Examples and Style

Covert brands like Dig Deep Documentary produce English-language, high-production content in classic RT style—sometimes literally repackaged RT videos. Influencer repost channels mirror talking-head commentary aligned with RT messaging goals without creator consent.

## Broader Implications

Butler notes similar tactics appear beyond RT, suggesting a shared playbook for evading platform bans. The talk highlights how state propaganda adapts to moderation by laundering identity through seemingly independent media brands.

talks.title: Unity of Hacktivist Fronts: Iranian Cyber-Enabled IO Targeting Israel
talks.teaser: Maps Iranian hacktivist fronts behind Israel-focused leak operations and the reused infrastructure that links them.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at Iranian cyber-enabled information operations that rose after the Israel-Hamas war began. The speaker focuses on hacktivist fronts that run Telegram-centred campaigns of doxxing, defacement and breach data posting. He describes a cluster of hack-and-leak operations that started before the war and walks through four of them in order. The first, Anzu Team, emerged in mid-2023 after Quran burnings in Sweden, published the names of those involved, and sent more than 15,000 text messages after compromising a Swedish telecom firm.

The later cases follow a similar pattern. The Cyber Court, formed in April 2024, issued verdicts against companies and organisations, and member groups then attacked them; several of those groups appear to have been created for this one operation. Zeus is Talking, in July 2024, leaked travel and personal data of an Israeli Olympic delegation, and Israel's national cyber directorate later linked it to Iran. A French false-flag persona, RGU France, sent threatening messages and a fake funeral invitation. Across the cluster, the speaker points to shared traits: onion hosting, prepositioned backup domains, IP logger tracking pixels, reused Iran-linked infrastructure and growing use of Russian hosting.

The takeaways are that these actors accept high exposure and keep returning after takedowns, and that their infrastructure habits can support attribution even without an official advisory. The speaker also suggests that the apparent lack of activity against US elections may reflect domain seizures or a stronger focus on Israel.

talks.title: Domain of Deception: How China's GLASSBRIDGE Campaign Manipulates the Web
talks.teaser: Maps a network of PR-run fake news sites pushing pro-China narratives, and how Google has enforced against them.
talks.summary:
A speaker from Google's TAG team introduces GLASSBRIDGE, a group of connected Chinese PR firms. Mandiant first linked dozens of domains spreading influence content to one such company, and later work found several hundred domains run by it. Google tracks the four firms as one actor because they share tactics and narratives, and together they run more than a thousand websites posing as independent outlets.

The sites republish PRC state media, such as Global Times articles on the South China Sea and Taiwan, along with press releases and content likely commissioned by other clients. Quality is poor: filler pieces on the metaverse recur across domains, and one site purporting to be Portuguese mixes languages under odd categories such as hotel and chicken. Others copy local news from legitimate sources in Brazil and Germany, and some republish content from the spammy Dragon Bridge network.

Because PR firms sit between sponsors and content, the actual customer stays hidden, giving plausible deniability. The speaker assesses that a shared customer may be behind the firms, though who hired them cannot be attributed. Google has made over a thousand of these domains ineligible for the Google News Corpus and will keep blocking the activity. The talk notes that Russia and Iran run similar fake local news domains, showing influence actors increasingly work beyond social media.

talks.title: COLDRIVER: Subversive and Swole
talks.teaser: Maps FSB-linked narrow phishing, split-domain credential traps, and tradecraft shifts after indictments and public reporting.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces Cold River, described as an FSB-linked cluster also tracked under names such as Star Blizzard and UNC4057. The group concentrates on Western Europe and the United States, with occasional interest in Russian opposition figures. Victims are usually NGOs, journalists, think tanks, government and military figures, retirees from intelligence roles, and NATO-adjacent academics. Campaigns lean on narrow, repeated contact rather than mass mail, often impersonating someone the target already knows and using convincing PDF lures hosted on cloud drives.

The middle of the talk walks through tradecraft: fake encrypted attachments that push victims toward drive links, paired front-and-back-end domains with headless browser checks, residential proxies for loading profile images on cloned login pages, HubSpot abuse, and predictable two-word domain naming that defenders once used for quick recognition. A late 2023 indictment and Microsoft reporting prompted changes—broken headless evasion, brief password-protected lures, then harder-to-guess domains, hCaptcha and later Cloudflare Turnstile on the front end, heavy Proton Mail sending, URL shorteners and open redirects, and fewer classic PDFs in the wild. Citizen Lab and Access Now coverage in August 2024 coincided with dropping headless code in favor of Turnstile. Continued compromises through 2024 included leaks attributed on Telegram, and the speaker notes newly attributed Rust malware called Spika delivered through the same social path.

Practitioners should treat high-risk users as Phishing-resistant authentication targets, watch for impersonation at personal inboxes, and contribute hashes and domains to protective feeds. The talk emphasizes that infrastructure tracing patterns still help when PDF hunting gets harder.

talks.title: Unveiling Operation Texonto: A Case Study of Russian Information Operations in Ukraine and Beyond
talks.teaser: Examines Russian Operation Texonto email waves in Ukraine and Russia, blending propaganda PDFs, phishing lures, and rented infrastructure.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames Operation Texonto as a contemporary influence effort aimed mainly at Ukrainians during the Russia–Ukraine war, comparable in intent to wartime leaflet drops but delivered over email and attached documents. Tracking began in November 2023 with messages impersonating the Ukrainian Ministry of Agriculture while discussing medicine shortages, plus PDFs that mixed ministries’ branding and original propaganda themes such as food scarcity.

Subsequent waves timed emails to front-line events: April 2024 messages urged Kyiv-region residents to leave by 15 April as Russian forces pressed near the city; a later Sumy-region push warned of strikes and utility cuts during a Ukrainian offensive. A November wave pushed narratives about mobilizing women, forged partisan-movement branding, and drew public warnings from the real Telegram channel being impersonated. The same operation also reached Russia, including election-eve mail meant to disrupt Navalny-team “noon” protest voting guidance via domains echoing Alexei Navalny’s name.

Beyond information operations, the speaker ties Texonto to credential phishing against a Ukrainian defense firm using a typosquatted Microsoft login domain, and to lures aimed at Europol-related contacts. The same registered infrastructure later carried Canadian pharmacy spam, supporting a model where criminal hosts rent capabilities across IO, phishing, and fraud. Attribution stays at Russian threat-actor level without naming individuals; defenders gain campaign timelines, impersonation quirks, and published IOCs from the team’s research.

talks.title: Should We Attribute Less? Foreign Interference Claims & the 2024 U.S. Election
talks.teaser: Compares foreign influence attributions from the 2020 and 2024 US election cycles, and the trade-offs of publicly naming them.
talks.summary:
The talk, from the Digital Forensic Research Lab, asks whether influence operation attributions should be made less often. Attribution can reveal actors' tactics and disrupt campaigns, but it can also spark panic, lack context or make an operation look bigger than it is. The lab's foreign interference attribution tracker covers the 2024 U.S. election cycle. Cases had to be primarily digital, novel or add new evidence, and relate to the 2024 election. Coding combined a human coder, a Claude-assisted second pass and a manual reconciliation, using a 63-variable taxonomy.

Government attributions made up half of the roughly 80 cases, about 40, and most were official actions such as Justice Department takedowns. The 2020 tracker had 33 government attributions, mostly drawn from media interviews and quotes. A pre-election government update offered warnings but lacked the specifics of named actions against named actors. Attributions also drew political reactions: a Justice Department action against Russian influence actors was read in different ways, and Russia's president responded with an ironic endorsement of a candidate. Leaked Social Design Agency documents suggested operators tracked attributions of their campaigns as performance metrics.

Overall, attribution volume and quality rose compared with 2020, while public search interest in the topic fell. The speaker called lower attention a good sign, but warned that government disclosure may shrink, leaving companies and nonprofits to keep the record public. Their answer to whether to attribute less was probably not.
